text: Imagine you go for a routine health check, and the doctor suggests a quick screening test.
visual: Line-art clinic door draws on; a small person icon walks to it; a clipboard with 'screening test' pops up.

text: It looks for a condition that is fairly rare. About one in every hundred people your age has it.
visual: 10 x 10 grid of person squares on axes (columns 1–10, rows 1–10); one square turns orange. Chip: '1 in 100 have it'.

text: The test is good. If you have the condition, it catches it nine times out of ten.
visual: Stat card 1: ten orange squares; nine get an aqua 'positive' ring. Caption 'catches 9 of 10 who have it'.

text: And if you are healthy, it only gives a false alarm one time in ten.
visual: Stat card 2: ten blue squares; one gets an aqua ring. Caption 'false alarm for 1 in 10 healthy people'.

text: A few days later, the result comes back. Positive.
visual: An envelope slides in and opens; 'POSITIVE' stamps on in aqua.

text: So, how worried should you be? What is the chance you actually have it?
visual: A probability meter appears: a horizontal axis 0%–100% with ticks every 10, title 'chance you have it'.

text: Take a second, and make your own guess.
visual: The meter waits; a blinking '?' cursor sits on it; tiny clock ticks.

text: Most people say about ninety percent. After all, the test is ninety percent accurate.
visual: A grey 'gut feeling' pointer slides to 90% on the meter.

text: Here's the surprise. The real answer is about eight percent.
visual: A violet pointer drops in at 8.3%; the grey 90% pointer is crossed out in red.

text: Not ninety. Eight. Less than one in ten.
visual: Big comparison: '90%' (grey, struck) vs '≈ 8%' (violet), camera pushes in on the violet number.

text: Nothing in that story is a trick. The test really is good. Your gut just left out one number.
visual: The three fact chips line up: '1 in 100 have it' · 'catches 9 of 10' · 'false alarm 1 in 10'.

text: How rare the condition was to begin with.
visual: The '1 in 100' chip turns warn yellow and glows: 'the base rate'.

text: The tool that puts that number back in is called Bayes' theorem. And by the end of this video, you will be able to do this in your head.
visual: Title card: 'BAYES' THEOREM' (violet) with subtitle 'explained simply, with real examples'.

text: Welcome to Math Lab TV. Where math is something you can see.
visual: Logo (violet rounded square with a green bell curve) + MATH LAB TV + tagline 'where math is something you can see'.

text: Today you will learn how to turn a test result into a real probability, just by counting people.
visual: Small logo moves top-right. Big ① (aqua); mini grid where 108 squares light up and 9 turn orange; caption 'turn a test result into a real probability'.

text: You will see Bayes' theorem as a formula, and exactly what every symbol means.
visual: Big ② (violet); the formula P(A|B) = P(B|A)·P(A) / P(B) writes on; caption 'the formula, symbol by symbol'.

text: And you will see how evidence adds up, in spam filters, fraud alerts and machine learning.
visual: Big ③ (warn); a mini meter walks 1% → 8% → 45%; caption 'how evidence adds up'.

text: This isn't just about medical tests.
visual: The clinic icon shrinks to the corner; three empty cards slide in.

text: Any time a rare thing meets an imperfect detector, the same trap is waiting.
visual: Equation of icons: 'rare thing' (orange dot) + 'imperfect detector' (aqua radar) = 'trap' (red).

text: A smoke alarm going off. An email flagged as spam. A message from your bank asking, was this you?
visual: Three cards fill in turn: smoke alarm, envelope with 'spam' tag, phone with 'Was this you?'.

text: Each one is a positive test. And each one asks the same question: given this alarm, how likely is the real thing?
visual: Each card gets an aqua 'positive' ring; a banner: 'given the alarm → how likely is the real thing?'.

text: And smart people get this wrong. In one well known study, doctors were given a screening puzzle with numbers like ours.
visual: Card 'Study of doctors · a screening puzzle like ours' (generic, no names or logos).

text: Only about one in five picked the right answer. Almost half picked nine in ten.
visual: Bar chart on axes, y 'share of doctors (%)' 0–50: bar 'about 1 in 10 (correct)' ≈ 21%, bar '9 in 10' ≈ 47%.

text: That's not because doctors are bad at math. It's because the numbers came as percentages of percentages.
visual: A jumble of '%' signs ('1%', '90%', '10%') swirl together.

text: Change the form, and the problem becomes easy. So here is the trick for this whole video: stop thinking in percentages, and start counting people.
visual: The '%' signs morph into a neat grid of person squares. Chip: 'count people'.

text: And Bayes isn't only about tests. It's a rule for changing your mind by the right amount when new evidence arrives. Not too little, and not too much.
visual: A dial labelled 'how sure am I?' turns a little, not all the way: 'update by the right amount'.

text: Let's do it. Picture one thousand people, all taking the same test.
visual: Axes appear: x 'column' 0–40 (ticks every 5), y 'row' 0–25 (ticks every 5), equal scale. A 40 x 25 grid of squares fills in, counter 0 → 1,000.

text: Each little square is one person. Forty across, twenty five down. One thousand.
visual: Camera zooms to the top-left corner: one square labelled 'one person'; then '40 × 25 = 1,000'.

text: Step one. How many of them have the condition? One in a hundred. So, ten people.
visual: Step chip '1'. Ten squares in the first column turn orange; counter '10 have it' (orange); warn tag 'base rate 1 in 100'.

text: The other nine hundred and ninety are healthy.
visual: The rest pulse blue; counter '990 healthy' (blue).

text: Step two. Test the ten people who have the condition. It catches nine of them.
visual: Step chip '2'. Camera zooms on the orange column; nine get aqua rings one by one.

text: So, nine true positives, and one person the test misses.
visual: Labels: '9 true positives' (aqua) and '1 missed' (muted) beside the column.

text: Step three. Test the nine hundred and ninety healthy people. It wrongly flags one in ten of them.
visual: Step chip '3'. Camera pulls back; aqua rings ripple across the blue squares, one in every ten.

text: That's ninety nine false alarms.
visual: Counter '99 false alarms' ticks up in aqua as the rings land.

text: Now, look only at the people holding a positive result.
visual: Everyone without a ring dims to 15%.

text: Nine of them actually have the condition. Ninety nine are healthy. One hundred and eight positives in total.
visual: The 108 ringed squares fly out into two stacks on new axes (y 'people who tested positive' 0–100, ticks every 20): an orange bar of 9 and a blue bar of 99, each built from countable squares.

text: If your test is positive, you are one of these one hundred and eight. And only nine of them are sick.
visual: A 'you are somewhere in here' bracket over both stacks; the orange 9 glows.

text: Nine out of one hundred and eight. That's one in twelve, about eight percent.
visual: Fraction 9 / 108 (LaTeX) = 1/12 ≈ 8.3%, in violet.

text: The test did its job. It caught almost everyone who was sick.
visual: Tick on '9 of 10 caught'.

text: But healthy people outnumber sick people ninety nine to one. So even a small false alarm rate creates a crowd of false alarms.
visual: Balance beam: left pan 10 orange, right pan 990 blue — beam crashes right. Then the pans swap to 9 vs 99 — still crashes right.

text: Here, the false alarms outnumber the real cases eleven to one.
visual: '99 ÷ 9 = 11' chip; eleven blue squares line up beside each orange one.

text: And yes, the test really is ninety percent accurate overall. Nine true positives, plus eight hundred and ninety one healthy people correctly cleared. Nine hundred right answers out of a thousand.
visual: Counter: '9 + 891 = 900 correct of 1,000 = 90% accurate' — the accuracy is real, it just answers a different question.

text: And notice, the positive result still mattered. Before the test, your chance was one in a hundred. After it, one in twelve.
visual: Probability meter 0–100% (ticks every 10, zoomed section 0–10%): warn pointer at 1%, violet pointer slides to 8.3%.

text: That's more than eight times higher. The test moved you a lot. It just didn't move you anywhere near certain.
visual: Arrow '× 8.3' between the pointers; a faint '100% certain' marker far right.

text: And a negative result? Of the eight hundred and ninety two people who test negative, just one has the condition.
visual: Back to the 1,000-grid: the 892 unringed squares light up; the one missed orange square blinks.

text: So a negative test drops your chance from one in a hundred to about one in nine hundred. That's very reassuring.
visual: Fraction 1 / 892 ≈ 0.1% (violet); meter pointer slides down from 1% to ~0.1%.

text: What we just did, counting people, is exactly Bayes' theorem. Let's write it the way you'll see it in books.
visual: The two stacks (9 and 99) shrink to the left side; a blank formula card appears on the right.

text: Here is the same crowd as a tree. One thousand people split into ten who have it, and nine hundred and ninety who don't.
visual: Tree diagram builds left to right: root '1,000' → branches '10 have it' (orange, 'x 1/100') and '990 healthy' (blue, 'x 99/100').

text: Then each branch splits again by the test result. Nine and one on top. Ninety nine and eight hundred and ninety one below.
visual: Second split: 10 → '9 positive' (aqua ring) / '1 negative'; 990 → '99 positive' (aqua ring) / '891 negative'. Branch labels 9/10, 1/10, 1/10, 9/10.

text: A positive result means you're on one of the two positive leaves. Nine, or ninety nine. That's all Bayes is doing.
visual: The two positive leaves glow; the others dim; bracket '9 of 108'.

text: First, the symbols. A capital P, with brackets, means the probability of whatever is inside.
visual: Definition card: 'P( … ) = the probability of …'.

text: A means having the condition. B means testing positive.
visual: Definition cards: 'A = has the condition' (orange), 'B = tests positive' (aqua).

text: And this vertical bar means given. So, P of A given B is the chance you have the condition, given that you tested positive.
visual: Definition card '| = given'. Then 'P(A | B) = chance you have it, given a positive test' (violet).

text: That's the number we want. And here is Bayes' theorem.
visual: The full formula writes on: P(A|B) = P(B|A) · P(A) / P(B).

text: P of A given B equals P of B given A, times P of A, divided by P of B.
visual: Each term brightens as it is read.

text: Now let's match each piece to our crowd.
visual: Dashed connectors from each term to the crowd stacks.

text: P of A is the base rate. How common the condition is before any test. Ten in a thousand.
visual: P(A) glows warn; below it '= 10 / 1000'.

text: P of B given A is how good the test is at catching it. Nine out of ten.
visual: P(B|A) glows aqua; '= 9 / 10'.

text: Multiply those two, and you get the true positives. Nine in a thousand.
visual: '9/10 × 10/1000 = 9/1000'; the orange stack of 9 pulses.

text: P of B, on the bottom, is the chance of testing positive at all. Real or false, that's one hundred and eight in a thousand.
visual: P(B) underlined; '= 108 / 1000'; both stacks pulse.

text: Divide, and the thousands cancel. Nine out of one hundred and eight. The same answer we got by counting.
So the formula is just a short way of saying: real positives, divided by all positives.
visual: Plain-words version under the formula: 'real positives ÷ all positives'.

text: The bottom part is where people slip. It hides the false alarms.
visual: P(B) splits open like a box: inside, '9 real' + '99 false alarms' (the 99 glowing).

text: Written out in full, P of B is the true positives from the sick, plus the false alarms from the healthy.
visual: Expanded: P(B) = P(B|A)·P(A) + P(B|not A)·P(not A); definition chip 'not A = healthy'; numbers 9/1000 + 99/1000.

text: Three names you'll hear. The base rate is called the prior. The answer is called the posterior. And P of B given A is called the likelihood.
visual: Labels attach to the formula: 'prior' (warn) under P(A), 'likelihood' (aqua) under P(B|A), 'posterior' (violet) under P(A|B).

text: Prior means before the evidence. Posterior means after.
visual: Timeline arrow: 'before evidence → after evidence', prior 1% → posterior 8.3%.

text: So you tested positive, and your chance is now about one in twelve. What would a sensible doctor do next?
visual: The violet '1 in 12' card; a second test tube icon slides in.

text: Test again. And here is the beautiful part. The answer from the first test becomes the starting point for the second.
visual: Loop arrow: posterior (violet) curls back around and becomes the new prior (warn).

text: Yesterday's posterior is today's prior.
visual: Text card with the loop arrow; 'posterior → prior'.

text: Take our one hundred and eight positives. Nine are sick, ninety nine are healthy. They all take a second test.
visual: The two stacks (9 orange, 99 blue) return on their axes.

text: To avoid fractions of people, picture ten times as many. Ninety people who have it, and nine hundred and ninety who don't.
visual: '× 10' badge; stacks rescale: y axis now 0–1,000, ticks every 200; bars 90 and 990.

text: The test catches nine in ten of the sick, and wrongly flags one in ten of the healthy. Same as before.
visual: Aqua rings sweep the bars: 90 → 81 kept; 990 → 99 kept.

text: After a second positive: eighty one sick, and ninety nine healthy.
visual: New bars: orange 81, blue 99 (axis 0–100, ticks every 20) — now nearly level.

text: Eighty one out of one hundred and eighty. That's forty five percent.
visual: Fraction 81 / 180 = 45% in violet.

text: One percent, then eight, then forty five. Each positive pushes the number up.
visual: Number-line walk on the meter 0–100%: pointer hops 1% → 8.3% → 45%.

text: There's a neat shortcut here. Compare sick to healthy as odds.
visual: Balance beam returns with 'odds = sick : healthy'.

text: Before any test, the odds are one sick person for every ninety nine healthy.
visual: Beam: 1 orange vs 99 blue → '1 : 99'.

text: A sick person is nine times more likely to test positive than a healthy one. Ninety percent, versus ten.
visual: '90% ÷ 10% = 9' chip, labelled 'likelihood ratio'.

text: So each positive multiplies the odds of having it by nine. One to ninety nine becomes nine to ninety nine, then eighty one to ninety nine.
visual: Odds ladder: 1 : 99 → × 9 → 9 : 99 → × 9 → 81 : 99; beam levels out step by step.

text: A third positive makes it seven hundred and twenty nine to ninety nine. About eighty eight percent.
visual: '729 : 99 → 729 / 828 ≈ 88%'; meter pointer hops to 88%. Beam tips toward 'sick'.

text: One important condition. This only works if the second test makes its mistakes independently of the first.
visual: Assumption card (white border): 'assumes the tests' errors are independent'.

text: If you repeat the same test on the same sample, it might simply repeat the same false alarm. Then the second positive tells you much less.
visual: Two identical test tubes; the same smudge on both → '= 1 clue, not 2'.

text: That's one reason doctors often confirm with a different kind of test.
visual: Second tube changes shape and colour: 'different method'.

text: So what actually moves the answer? There are only three dials. The base rate, the hit rate, and the false alarm rate.
visual: Three dials: 'base rate' (warn) at 1 in 100, 'hit rate' (aqua) at 9 in 10, 'false alarm rate' (blue) at 1 in 10.

text: Let's turn the base rate dial first, and keep the test exactly the same.
visual: Axes: x 'base rate (%)' 0–50 (ticks every 10), y 'chance you have it after a positive (%)' 0–100 (ticks every 20).

text: At one in a hundred, we're at eight percent. At one in ten, it jumps to fifty percent.
visual: A violet curve traces from left; dots pinned at (1, 8.3) and (10, 50) with labels.

text: Let's check that middle one by counting. With one in ten, a thousand people means one hundred sick, and the test catches ninety of them.
visual: Mini crowd: 100 orange squares (ten columns of the 40 x 25 grid), 90 ringed aqua.

text: Nine hundred healthy, and one in ten flagged. Ninety false alarms. Ninety real, ninety false. Fifty percent.
visual: 900 blue, 90 ringed; two equal stacks 90 | 90 on axes 0–100; '90 / 180 = 50%' violet.

text: And only when half the people have the condition does your gut's ninety percent finally become right.
visual: Curve reaches (50, 90); a grey 'gut: 90%' dashed line meets it there.

text: The rarer the condition, the more the false alarms win.
visual: Left end of the curve highlighted; '1 in 100 → 8%'.

text: Now turn the false alarm dial instead. Same base rate, one in a hundred, but a test that wrongly flags only one healthy person in a hundred.
visual: False-alarm dial turns from 1 in 10 to 1 in 100; the blue stack of 99 shrinks.

text: Now there are about ten false alarms instead of ninety nine, and a positive means about forty eight percent.
visual: Stacks: orange 9 vs blue 9.9 (≈10); '9 / 18.9 ≈ 48%' in violet.

text: And the hit rate dial? Push it from nine in ten all the way to perfect, and the answer barely moves. From about eight percent to about nine.
visual: Hit-rate dial turns to 10 of 10; orange stack 9 → 10; '10 / 109 ≈ 9%'.

text: So, a rule of thumb. When the thing you're looking for is rare, the false alarm rate matters far more than the hit rate.
visual: Rule-of-thumb card: 'rare thing → false alarm rate matters most' (labelled 'rule of thumb').

text: Now let's see where this shows up in the real world. The labels change, but the counting is the same.
visual: Four domain tiles: ML, DS, FINANCE, CS.

text: Machine learning. A classifier is just a test run by a computer.
visual: ML tile expands: input dots → model box → 'positive' / 'negative' outputs.

text: Engineers have names for our numbers. Catching nine out of ten sick people is called recall.
visual: 'recall = 9 / 10 = 90%' (aqua), with the orange column of 10 and 9 rings.

text: And nine out of one hundred and eight, the share of alarms that are real, is called precision.
visual: 'precision = 9 / 108 ≈ 8%' (violet), with the two stacks.

text: When the thing you're looking for is rare, a model can have great recall and still terrible precision. That's the base rate at work.
visual: Two gauges side by side: recall 90% (full), precision 8% (nearly empty).

text: That's why teams measure precision on data with the real base rate. On a balanced test set, half positive and half negative, our same test would show ninety percent precision. In the real world, about eight percent.
visual: Two panels: 'balanced test set (50% positive) → precision 90%' vs 'real world (1% positive) → precision 8%'.

text: And here's a trap. A model that simply says healthy to everyone is ninety nine percent accurate, and completely useless.
visual: Grid of 1,000 all marked 'healthy': '990 / 1000 correct = 99% accuracy' with a red '0 of 10 caught'.

text: Data science. Bayes is the engine of Bayesian statistics.
visual: DS tile expands.

text: You start with a prior belief, say, about how often visitors to a website buy something, and update it as each day's data comes in.
visual: Axes x 'purchase rate (%)' 0–10, y 'belief (shape only)': a wide warn curve narrows into a violet curve as day-1, day-2, day-3 data chips arrive. Labelled 'shape only'.

text: Each day's posterior becomes the next day's prior. Exactly like our second test.
visual: Loop arrow posterior → prior, as in the Test Again chapter.

text: And before trusting any automated flag on a dashboard, a good analyst asks: of all the past flags, how many were real? That's precision again, measured on real data.
visual: Dashboard card with a column of past flags: few aqua-ringed orange (real), many blue (false); 'real ÷ all flags'.

text: Finance. Banks run fraud detectors on card payments.
visual: Finance tile expands: card + payment stream.

text: Fraud is rare, far rarer than one in a hundred payments. So even a detector as good as our test would flag mostly honest payments.
visual: Same 1,000-grid relabelled 'payments', with even fewer orange squares; aqua flags land mostly on blue ('honest').

text: That's one reason many banks send a quick, was this you, message instead of simply blocking the card. In Bayes terms, your reply is a second, independent test.
visual: Phone with 'Was this you?' → reply 'Yes' → meter drops / 'No' → meter jumps.

text: The same idea applies to market signals. A warning sign that fired before most crashes may also fire in many calm years. Always ask how often it fires when nothing happens.
visual: Timeline of years (axis 'year 1–20', generic, labelled 'illustration'): signal flags on several years, only two of them crash years.

text: Computer science. Some of the first really effective spam filters were built on Bayes' theorem.
visual: CS tile expands: inbox with a spam folder.

text: The prior is how much of all email is spam. The evidence is the words inside.
visual: Email card; words 'FREE', 'winner', 'meeting' highlighted; prior chip 'share of email that is spam'.

text: Each word nudges the odds up or down, just like each positive test. The filter multiplies them together.
visual: Odds ladder like before: '× (FREE)' up, '× (meeting)' down. Each arrow labelled 'shape only' factors.

text: To keep it simple, it treats every word as independent of the others. That shortcut is why it's called naive Bayes. It isn't true, but it works surprisingly well.
visual: 'naive Bayes = assume words are independent' card; a check mark 'works surprisingly well'.

text: Computer security has the same problem. An intrusion alarm that fires on just one in a thousand normal logins can still bury the few real attacks under false alarms.
visual: Login stream: thousands of blue login dots, rare orange attack dots; aqua alarms mostly on blue.

text: Before we wrap up, here are the three most common mistakes people make with Bayes.
visual: Three red cards face down.

text: Mistake one: flipping the question.
visual: Card 1 flips: 'Flipping the question'.

text: The chance of a positive test, if you're sick, is ninety percent. The chance you're sick, if you test positive, is about eight percent.
visual: P(B | A) = 90% (aqua) above P(A | B) ≈ 8% (violet); the A and B letters swap places.

text: Same words, swapped around. Completely different numbers.
visual: Red swap arrows between the two; '90% ≠ 8%'.

text: In courtrooms, this flip has a name: the prosecutor's fallacy. The chance of the evidence if someone is innocent is not the chance they're innocent, given the evidence.
visual: Scales of justice icon; two cards 'P(evidence | innocent)' vs 'P(innocent | evidence)' with '≠'.

text: Mistake two: ignoring the base rate.
visual: Card 2 flips: 'Ignoring the base rate'.

text: Take the same test, but give it only to patients who already have symptoms. Say one in five of them has the condition.
visual: Same 40 x 25 grid; now 200 squares (five columns) turn orange; warn tag 'base rate 1 in 5'.

text: Out of a thousand, that's one hundred and eighty true positives, against eighty false alarms. Now a positive means about seventy percent.
visual: Stacks: orange 180 vs blue 80 (axis 0–200, ticks every 50); '180 / 260 ≈ 69%' in violet.

text: Same test. Same result. The base rate changed everything.
visual: Side by side: 'base rate 1 in 100 → 8%' vs 'base rate 1 in 5 → 69%'.

text: Mistake three: counting the same clue twice.
visual: Card 3 flips: 'Counting a clue twice'.

text: If two tests share the same weakness, or two news stories copy the same source, they are really one piece of evidence, not two.
visual: Two news cards with arrows back to one source card.

text: Multiply them as if they were independent, and you'll end up far too confident.
visual: Meter pointer overshoots to 88% (red 'overconfident'), then settles back toward 8% with '1 clue'.

text: And a bonus mistake: deciding the test is useless because the answer was only eight percent.
visual: Red card 'Bonus: “the test is useless”'.

text: It isn't. A positive raised the chance more than eightfold, and a negative almost rules the condition out. A good test is a strong clue. It's just not a verdict.
visual: Meter: 1% → 8.3% (positive) and 1% → 0.1% (negative), both arrows big.

text: Let's turn all of that into a recipe you can use for any yes or no question.
visual: Recipe card frame unrolls: 'Bayes in five steps'.

text: Step one: start with the base rate. How common is the thing, before any evidence?
visual: Item 1 (warn): 'Start with the base rate' + 'how common is it before any evidence?'.

text: Step two: picture a crowd. One thousand people usually avoids fractions.
visual: Item 2: 'Picture a crowd' + 'e.g. 1,000 people'.

text: Step three: split the crowd with the test. Count the true positives, and the false alarms.
visual: Item 3 (aqua): 'Split by the test' + 'true positives and false alarms'.

text: Step four: keep only the people who match the evidence, and divide. Real cases, over all positives.
visual: Item 4 (violet): 'Keep the matches and divide' + 'real ÷ all positives'.

text: Step five: update. When new, independent evidence arrives, your answer becomes the new base rate.
visual: Item 5: 'Update' + 'posterior becomes the next prior'.

text: For our test: one in a hundred to start. Nine real positives, ninety nine false alarms. About eight percent.
visual: Summary strip under the card: '1 in 100 → 9 real vs 99 false → 9/108 ≈ 8%'.

text: A test result is a clue, not a verdict. Bayes tells you how much the clue is worth.
visual: Closing line types on in violet, centred.

text: Look around your world, and notice how many alarms are false alarms, and how rare the real thing usually is.
visual: Four everyday cards: smoke alarm, car alarm, spam folder, 'was this you?' text — each stamped 'real or false alarm?'.

text: If this lesson made things clear for you, please subscribe to Math Lab TV, so we can keep building together.
visual: Logo + red SUBSCRIBE button; a cursor clicks it; it turns grey 'SUBSCRIBED ✓'; 'so we can keep building together' appears.

text: But here's a puzzle for next time.
visual: Small logo stays top-centre; a puzzle-piece icon draws on.

text: Scientists often report a number called a p-value, and it's very often described as the chance that a result is a fluke.
visual: Card 'p = 0.03' with a speech bubble 'a 3% chance it's a fluke?' and a red question mark.

text: That description flips the question, just like mistake one.
visual: The two flipped cards from mistake one reappear: 'P(data | no effect)' vs 'P(no effect | data)'.

text: Next time, we'll see what a p-value really measures, and why Bayes is the missing piece.
visual: Chip 'next: p-values' appears under the small logo.

text: I will see you in the next video.
visual: Logo + 'next: p-values' chip hold.
